records.text: The main advantage of convolutional neural networks is weight reuse.
In convolutional neural networks, the same weights are applied over the entire input.
The same weights are applied across all intermediate feature tensors (outputs of intermediate layers).
Weight reuse enables parallel processing.
Weight reuse drastically reduces the number of parameters.

In classical computer vision, before neural networks, convolutions were used as handcrafted filters applied in parallel over an image for tasks such as sharpening, blurring, adding contrast, embossing, and edge detection.
Gabor filters perform directed edge detection by computing discrete derivatives (finite differences) in different directions.
One Gabor filter activates on large vertical differences between adjacent pixels.
Another Gabor filter activates on horizontal changes.
Applying max pooling as an image filter clamps to maximum brightness and produces a strange result.
Applying average pooling as an image filter appears smoother.
The purpose of average pooling is not to produce a smoother image.
In ResNet-18, the first layer’s convolutional filters can be examined.
Some first-layer filters in ResNet-18 detect diagonal or vertical lines.
Other first-layer filters in ResNet-18 identify colors or color gradients.
With an input image, one first-layer filter in ResNet-18 might fire where green appears (e.g., grass or trees).
Another first-layer filter might fire for horizontal edges.
Deeper in ResNet-18, the direct pixel-to-feature correspondence vanishes.
Deeper in ResNet-18, each feature has a receptive field.
Pinpointing the exact contributing pixels for a deep feature requires additional math.
It is possible to observe what upper-layer features in ResNet-18 respond to.
In ResNet-18, the second layer fires for high-frequency content such as stripes and edges across the image.
Deeper layers in ResNet-18 activate for more semantic, salient objects.
A deep filter in ResNet-18 might fire for eyes and ear tips.
Even deeper filters in ResNet-18 respond to entire heads.
Visualizations of deep features become increasingly blurry and less geometric.
Deep features can be mapped back to the original image to approximate their triggers.
At a deep layer in ResNet-18, one can find features strongly selective for specific classes.
Cat-selectivity in ResNet-18 means that the feature’s activation correlates strongly with the 'cat' class, as trained on ImageNet.
Inputting a half-cat, half-dog image causes the cat-selective feature to fire on the cat half.
Inputting a half-cat, half-dog image causes the dog-selective feature to fire on the dog half.
GradCAM is a more detailed interpretation method.
In a classification network, the output is a set of probabilities per class.
Running GradCAM on a specific class output reveals which pixels contributed most to that output value.
For instance, in GradCAM, the 'Egyptian cat' output responds due to certain image pixels.
GradCAM is not an attention mechanism.
GradCAM provides an explanation for the network's decision.
In the cat-dog image, the Egyptian cat output focuses on cat pixels.
In the cat-dog image, the Blenheim-Spaniel output focuses on dog pixels.
AlexNet was the most important convolutional architecture in history.
AlexNet was the first truly effective convolutional network.
AlexNet dominated the ImageNet large-scale visual recognition competition by an extraordinary margin.
In 2011/2012, competing methods in the ImageNet competition had error rates around 22–23%.
AlexNet achieved an error rate of approximately 13% in the ImageNet competition.
The following year, the entire ImageNet leaderboard switched to convolutional networks.
After AlexNet, classical computer vision was abandoned for image classification.
AlexNet’s first key technical idea is that it is split into two parallel streams.
AlexNet was the first industrial-scale instance of model parallelization.
Model parallelization is a very important concept in deep learning.
To train with multiple GPUs, there are two main approaches: data parallelization and model parallelization.
Data parallelization splits a mini-batch across GPUs.
In data parallelization, the mini-batch parts are processed in parallel on different GPUs.
In data parallelization, the results from GPUs are collected.
In data parallelization, a single update is performed based on all weight updates.
In data parallelization, the network implementation does not change.
Data parallelization increases the effective mini-batch size by spreading the batch.
Model parallelization assumes the model does not fit on one GPU.
In model parallelization, you split the model across GPUs.
AlexNet, implemented by Alex Krizhevsky in 2011 and published in 2012, used model parallelization by hand.
Implementing model parallelization by hand was a major engineering feat at the time.
Today, frameworks like PyTorch allow assigning specific weight matrices to specific GPUs.
PyTorch automatically handles communication in model parallelization.
When designing a model-parallel network, you want to minimize cross-GPU communication because it is slower than on-chip communication.
For instance, a model-parallel design might have only two points where the GPUs exchange information.
AlexNet was the breakthrough moment for convolutional networks.
After AlexNet, the field of convolutional networks exploded.
Many improvements in convolutional networks followed from relatively simple ideas.
The first improvement after AlexNet was VGG.
AlexNet used $11 \times 11$ convolutions in the first layer.
Now we rarely see $11 \times 11$ convolutions.
VGG showed that large convolutions can be represented as compositions of small ones, typically stacks of $3 \times 3$ (sometimes $5 \times 5$).
Using stacks of small convolutions instead of large ones is like a convolution inside a convolution.
Using stacks of small convolutions further reduces the number of weights.
Using stacks of small convolutions acts as additional structural regularization.
Structural regularization from small convolution stacks works because the network processes different parts of the input in the same way.
VGG's approach usually works better than using large convolutions.
The second improvement idea is Inception (GoogLeNet).
Inception is part of the broader concept of Network in Network.
In Network in Network, an image tile is processed by a small neural network consisting of a single weight matrix applied to the concatenated input.
The inception trick replaces the simple convolution in a Network-in-Network with a more complex mini-network.
The inception mini-network is still applied identically across tiles.
Inception units often feature multiple parallel processing branches.
The use of multiple parallel branches in inception units is not a coincidence.
The third and most important improvement idea is residual connections.
Residual connections give rise to ResNet.
If a layer’s output $f(x)$ saturates, its gradients vanish.
Without a skip connection, if a layer's gradients vanish, all layers below stop receiving gradients because gradients flow through derivatives that go to zero.
The residual connection adds the input to the output: $y = f(x) + x$.
When $f(x)$ stops learning, gradients still flow through the identity path.
Kaiming He introduced ResNets.
Kaiming He called ResNets the 'revolution of depth.'
With residual connections, networks with hundreds of layers could be trained.
AlexNet had 8 trainable layers.
VGG had 19 trainable layers.
GoogLeNet had 22 trainable layers.
ResNet immediately reached 150 layers.
With residual connections, you could go to 200, 500, or even 1000 layers without training issues.
The only limit to increasing depth with residual connections is diminishing returns.
Practical ResNets go to about 200 layers.
The bottleneck idea reduces weight count further, similar to VGG.
VGG replaced a large $n \times n$ convolution, which has $n^2$ weights, by a sequence of small convolutions, which have linear in $n$ weights.
Convolutions already save a huge number of weights.
We can reduce weight count even further.
The input to a standard convolutional layer is a 3D tensor.
In a standard convolutional layer, the operation is replicated over the full input.
In a standard convolutional layer, a cut-out window has depth $D$, width $W$, and height $H$.
A standard convolutional layer produces a single feature vector of size $D'$.
The weight tensor of a standard convolutional layer has dimensions $D \times W \times H \times D'$.
The convolutional layer has far fewer parameters than a fully connected layer.
The parameter count of a convolutional layer can still grow quickly.
For a convolutional layer with $D = 256$, $D' = 256$, and $W = H = 3$, the weight tensor is $256 \times 3 \times 3 \times 256$, which is about 590K parameters.
Instead of a full convolution with $D \times D' \times 9$ weights, the bottleneck idea first compresses the features with a $1 \times 1$ convolution.
After the $1 \times 1$ compression, the bottleneck idea does the spatial convolution.
After the spatial convolution, the bottleneck idea expands back with another $1 \times 1$ convolution.
In the bottleneck idea, an input of size $D \times W \times H$ is passed through a $1 \times 1$ convolution that reduces depth to $D''$, for example 32.
Then a spatial convolution of size $W \times H$ is applied.
Finally, another $1 \times 1$ convolution restores the depth to $D'$, for example 256.
The parameter count of the bottleneck block is $D \cdot D'' + D'' \cdot W \cdot H \cdot D'' + D'' \cdot D'$.
For $D=256$, $D''=32$, $W=3$, $H=3$, the parameter count is $256 \times 32 + 32 \times 32 \times 9 + 32 \times 256 = 25,600$.
The original full convolution parameter count is approximately 590,000.
The bottleneck block achieves about a 25-fold saving in parameters.
In a single-branch bottleneck, a 256-dimensional feature vector is compressed to 32 numbers.
The decompression from 32 numbers back to 256 cannot restore the lost information.
In a single branch, the bottleneck idea makes no sense.
One could simply let the previous layer produce 32 features instead and save even more weights.
The bottleneck idea alone does not work.
The bottleneck idea never appears alone in practice.
The bottleneck idea becomes useful when multiple parallel branches are used.
In the split-transform-merge approach, several copies of the bottleneck block are created.
Each parallel branch has its own independently learned weights.
The outputs of the parallel branches are concatenated.
With $D=256$ and bottleneck $D''=32$, eight parallel branches are needed to reconstruct a 256-dimensional output.
The total parameter count for eight branches is approximately 205,000.
This results in about a 3–4-fold saving compared to the original 590,000 parameters.
Geometrically, the parallel branches take multiple different projections of the same high-dimensional feature space.
Each projection captures a different aspect of the data.
The split-transform-merge network can be trained to avoid losing important information.
The split-transform-merge network can even outperform processing the entire high-dimensional object at once.
Doing many random projections of a high-dimensional object is often a good idea.
In the split-transform-merge, the projections are learned to be useful, which is even better.
The approach is called split-transform-merge.
In split-transform-merge, first the input is split, then each part is transformed, then the results are merged.
Split-transform-merge is a standard idea in convolutional architectures.
ResNeXt is an example of split-transform-merge.
ResNeXt is now outdated, about 10 years old.
In ResNeXt, 256 channels are split into 32 paths of width 4.
ResNeXt implements multiple extreme projections that work better together.
The Inception and Inception-ResNet families were a highly important line of networks.
For a long time, Inception and Inception-ResNet served as the best backbones for various computer vision tasks.
When tackling tasks like object detection or segmentation, there is rarely enough labeled data to train a network from scratch.
The standard practice is to use a backbone pretrained on ImageNet for classification.
The classification head of the pretrained backbone is cut off.
The rest of the network is used as a feature extractor.
The feature extractor may be fine-tuned slightly.
The Inception-ResNet family was one of the most influential backbones around 2016.
The main idea of Inception-ResNet was to design progressively better basic blocks.
Basic blocks are small neural networks that process the inputs.
Another important advance was replacing pooling layers with learnable reduction blocks.
Max pooling can be used to reduce spatial dimension, e.g., from 256×256 to 128×128.
It is better to let a trainable layer do more interesting work for spatial reduction.
Trainable reduction is achieved by composing layers with strided convolutions so that the output becomes smaller.
Reduction blocks sometimes contain pooling internally.
Reduction blocks follow the split-transform-merge pattern.
In reduction blocks, several parallel processing lines produce results that are merged.
Adding residual connections to Inception yields Inception-ResNet.
Inception-ResNet V2 was a very influential and widely used backbone.
There were ideas to further reduce network size and the number of layers.
Two objectives must be balanced: memory (number of weights) and latency (number of layers).
A smaller network reduces memory.
Latency depends more on the number of layers because operations within a layer are parallelized on the GPU.
The number of sequential steps matters most for latency.
The size of intermediate representations also plays a role in latency.
Latency is critical for real-time applications such as surveillance tracking.
Surveillance tracking must run at least 30–60 fps.
SqueezeNet targeted efficiency goals.
MobileNet targeted efficiency goals.
MobileNet was designed specifically to bring computer vision to mobile devices.
EfficientNet topped the architectural progress in efficient convolutional networks.
EfficientNet's design was found automatically via large-scale neural architecture search.
The neural architecture search considered how to scale a convolutional network.
The three main scaling knobs are depth (number of layers), width (number of channels), and resolution (input size).
When scaling, if depth grows exponentially with exponent α, width with β, and resolution with γ, the total number of weights scales as their product.
They ran an evolutionary search to find the optimal balance of α, β, and γ.
The resulting EfficientNet family defined the state of the art across the field.
In the plot, the x-axis is the number of parameters (fewer is better).
In the plot, the y-axis is ImageNet top-1 accuracy (higher is better).
The best networks lie in the top left corner of the plot, representing small size and high accuracy.
Large networks generally achieve higher accuracy than small networks, indicating a trade-off.
The Pareto frontier shows, for each model size, the highest accuracy achievable.
The Pareto frontier shows, for each target accuracy, the smallest model size needed.
The EfficientNet family achieved state-of-the-art performance across all sizes, effectively defining the Pareto frontier.
Since the introduction of EfficientNet, there has been no revolution in convolutional network architectures.
The research community has largely switched to using transformers.
EfficientNet remains the best underlying convolutional architecture.
EfficientNet serves as the backbone for many object detection and segmentation pipelines.
Those pipelines achieve state-of-the-art results.
Batch normalization computes the mean of a feature over spatial dimensions and mini-batch examples.
Layer normalization does not average over the mini-batch dimension.
In layer normalization, with batch size one, normalization is performed over all features of a single sample, producing one statistic per layer.
Transformers commonly use layer normalization because they are large and often trained with small mini-batches.
Layer norm provides normalization within a single training sample.
Before transformers, the two main deep learning architectures were convolutional networks and recurrent networks.
Recurrent networks are designed for sequential data.
Images are two-dimensional structures, making CNNs a natural choice.
Input data often comes as sequences.
Time series data (e.g., financial data) is a sequence.
Sound is a sequence of amplitude ticks.
In classical ML, raw amplitude sequences are too long to process directly.
Sound is often preprocessed by cutting into 20-30 ms packets and extracting features, resulting in a sequence of feature vectors.
Text is a sequence of tokens with a one-dimensional structure.
Sequence-to-single output tasks, like text classification, take a sequence (e.g., news article) and output one label (e.g., topic).
Sequence generation tasks take a non-sequential input (like an image) and produce an output sequence (like a caption).
Sequence-to-sequence problems have both input and output as sequences, e.g., machine translation.
Sequence labeling produces an output sequence aligned with the input, such as part-of-speech tagging.
Subtitle generation from video is a sequence labeling task where each frame gets corresponding text.
Object tracking is a sequence labeling task where segmentation is applied per frame to track an object.
CNNs are not inherently well-suited for sequences.
Convolutional approaches to NLP were competitive with recurrent approaches before transformers became dominant.
CNNs lack the ability to recall information from long past in a sequence, which is necessary for understanding full sentences.
Understanding a paragraph requires remembering earlier context.
In RNNs, each input $x_t$ is processed by a small neural network called a recurrent unit.
The recurrent unit takes a new input $x$ and a hidden state $h$ as inputs.
The unit updates the hidden state to capture the sequence up to the current input, assuming the previous hidden state captured earlier context.
The recurrent unit is defined as a function $f(x, h)$ that outputs an updated hidden state $h'$ and optionally an output.
The hidden state is a vector that accumulates relevant information about the sequence.
The hidden state is initialized as $h_0$, then updated to $h_1, h_2,$ etc.
In classical RNNs, the hidden state update is $h' = g(Ax + Bh)$, with weight matrices $A$ and $B$ and activation $g$ (e.g., tanh, ELU).
RNNs date back to the late 1980s.
Initially, RNNs could not be trained properly due to insufficient compute.
A unidirectional RNN processes the sequence from left to right.
For whole-sequence classification, using the final hidden state of a unidirectional RNN may be sufficient.
For sequence labeling like part-of-speech tagging, a unidirectional RNN only sees preceding context, which is limiting.
Bidirectional RNNs consist of two separate RNNs: one processing left-to-right, the other right-to-left.
The two hidden states from bidirectional RNNs are merged to predict $y_t$, incorporating both past and future context.
Bidirectional RNNs should be used unless the task prohibits it.
Language modeling requires a unidirectional model because it predicts the next word from left context only.
Real-time object tracking may require a unidirectional network due to limited future visibility.
In sequence-to-sequence tasks, bidirectional RNNs are standard because the full input can be read before output.
In RNN training for sequence classification, the loss is computed from the final output prediction compared to the true label.
In an RNN, the weights (e.g., matrix $W$) are shared across all time steps.
Separate weight matrices per time step would make training infeasible.
Weight sharing enables processing sequences of arbitrary length.
The gradient w.r.t. a weight $w$ is the sum of its influence over all time steps: $\frac{\partial L}{\partial w_t} + \frac{\partial L}{\partial w_{t-1}} + \dots + \frac{\partial L}{\partial w_1}$.
The weight is reused at each time step in the computational graph, not separate weights.
Weight sharing, as in CNNs, allows sparse activations to build meaningful gradients.
In a simplified linear recurrence without activations or inputs, the hidden state evolves as $H_T = W^T H_0$.
The spectral radius $\rho$ of $W$ controls the scaling: $\|H_t\| \approx \rho^t \|H_0\|$.
If $\rho > 1$, activations explode exponentially, causing numerical overflow.
In the backward pass, multiplication by $W^\top$ similarly leads to sensitivity to $\rho$.
Exploding gradients occur when $\rho > 1$; vanishing gradients occur when $\rho < 1$.
Vanishing gradients cause loss of long-term memory because early inputs' influence decays exponentially.
Exploding gradients cause training failure; vanishing gradients degrade performance but are not catastrophic.
Exploding gradients can be fixed by gradient clipping.
If the gradient norm exceeds a threshold, scale it down to the threshold.
Clipping is applied repeatedly during training.
Gradient clipping is the only solution needed for exploding gradients.
Pascanu published a paper in 2013 studying RNN behavior.
The Pascanu paper provides insights into activation and weight dynamics during RNN training, not new architectures.
In the loss landscape, exploding gradients correspond to a region with a steep cliff where gradients become huge.
Without clipping, large gradients cause divergence.
With clipping, the updates stay in a normal regime and proceed in roughly the right direction.
Gradient clipping is a theoretically and practically sound method that preserves the descent direction.
